summary: Documents BSD rlogin, which provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal with proper flushing of output. It describes an existing widely used protocol and is informational. It was replaced by RFC 1282.

eli5.summary: It lets you sit at one computer and type on another. This is an old way to do that.

questions: how is rlogin different from telnet
how does rlogin handle window size
subtitle: A remote login protocol that transmits Unix terminal semantics better than Telnet.

tldr.problem: Telnet provides basic remote terminal access but does not carry Unix terminal features like flow control, window size changes, or cooked/raw mode switching.
tldr.mechanism: BSD rlogin is a protocol that runs over TCP (port 513) with a simpler initial handshake and in-band control messages to handle flow control, terminal modes, window size changes, and proper output flushing.
tldr.outcome: Rlogin became widely used on Unix systems as a superior alternative to Telnet, though it has security implications if password-bypass trusted-host features are misconfigured.

today: RFC 1258 is informational and was replaced by RFC 1282. Rlogin has largely been superseded by SSH due to security concerns, though it illustrates important Unix terminal semantics that later remote access protocols inherited.

sections.title: What Rlogin Provides
sections.content:
The rlogin facility provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal connection. It is widely used between Unix hosts because it transmits more of the Unix terminal environment semantics than Telnet and can be configured not to require password entry from trusted hosts. Rlogin uses TCP and requires connection to port 513.

The protocol assumes an eight-bit transparent stream. It handles local flow control (the client interprets start/stop characters to pause output), proper output flushing, and window size negotiation so remote programs know the terminal dimensions.
sections.eli5: Rlogin connects to another Unix computer over TCP and pretends to be a real terminal, understanding Unix terminal commands.

sections.title: Connection Establishment and Control
sections.content:
When a rlogin client connects, it sends four null-terminated strings: an empty string, the client username, the server username, and the terminal type/speed (e.g., "vt100/9600"). The server replies with a zero byte once it has received these and is ready for data transfer. After this, the client and server exchange window size information if the server supports it. The window change sequence is 12 bytes: two 0xFF bytes as a magic cookie, two lowercase 's' bytes, and 8 bytes of 16-bit values for rows, columns, and pixel dimensions in network byte order.

Control messages are embedded in the data stream using TCP's urgent-data pointer. The client can define an escape character (usually tilde) to issue local commands like suspension or connection termination.
sections.eli5: First, the two computers exchange names and what kind of terminal it is. Then they can talk about window size. The client has a secret escape key to send local commands.

sections.title: Data Flow and Mode Control
sections.content: In "cooked" mode (the default), the client intercepts start (ASCII DC1) and stop (DC3) characters to control output flow locally, sending all other characters to the host. In "raw" mode, start and stop are sent to the host, letting it decide their meaning. The server sends control bytes via TCP urgent data: 0x02 flushes buffered output, 0x10 switches to raw mode, and 0x20 switches back to cooked mode. These control bytes are not displayed to the user.
sections.eli5: In cooked mode, the local computer controls "pause" and "resume". In raw mode, the remote computer does. The server can force mode switches.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content: Rlogin allows trusted-host password bypass: a user can configure a .rhosts file listing hosts and users allowed to log in without a password. While convenient, this represents a security weakness that has been exploited. If one system is compromised, all systems in the trust relationship are accessible. The danger is magnified if password bypass is allowed between multiple systems. A compromise to the domain name server or network itself could allow a malicious host to impersonate a trusted system. Modern secure alternatives like Kerberos can mitigate these risks while preserving convenience.
sections.eli5: Rlogin can skip passwords for trusted computers. If one trusted computer gets hacked, the hacker can reach all the others. Be careful setting this up.
